cards.front: Why can antimicrobials be used against an infection without harming the patient?
cards.back: They act on a target the microbe has but human cells lack, such as the bacterial cell wall, bacterial folate synthesis, or a microbial enzyme with high affinity for the drug. This is selective toxicity.

cards.front: When should surgical prophylaxis be given, and when should it stop?
cards.back: Give it so that effective tissue levels are present at incision and throughout the procedure: oral agents about 1 hour before, IV agents just before or at induction (GG14: IV within 60 minutes before incision), with a repeat IV dose in long operations. Keep it short. Giving it more than 4 hours after wound closure is justified only for contaminated and dirty surgery, for up to 5 days.

cards.front: Give one narrow-spectrum and one broad-spectrum antibiotic.
cards.back: Narrow: penicillin G or streptomycin. Broad: tetracyclines or chloramphenicol. The line between them is now blurred, so the terms are a matter of degree.

cards.front: Which four antimicrobial groups are most often implicated in hypersensitivity?
cards.back: Penicillins, cephalosporins, sulfonamides and fluoroquinolones. The reactions are unpredictable, not dose related, and range from rash to anaphylaxis.

cards.front: What is meant by a low therapeutic index, and which agents have very low indices?
cards.back: The margin between effective and toxic dose is narrow, so dosing must be individualised and monitored. Polymyxin B and amphotericin B have very low indices, so they are reserved for cases with no alternative. Aminoglycosides, vancomycin, tetracyclines and chloramphenicol have lower margins than penicillins or erythromycin.

cards.front: How do natural resistance and acquired resistance differ?
cards.back: Natural resistance is a trait of a whole species or group, for example gram-negative bacilli and penicillin G, or anaerobes and aminoglycosides; it rarely matters clinically. Acquired resistance develops in a previously sensitive strain after drug exposure and is a major clinical problem.

cards.front: Contrast vertical and horizontal transfer of resistance.
cards.back: Vertical transfer is selection of pre-existing mutants when the drug kills sensitive cells; it is slow and usually low grade, as with a single anti-TB drug. Horizontal transfer moves resistance genes between bacteria by conjugation (plasmids and R factors), transduction by phage, or transformation. It is fast and can spread multidrug resistance at once.

cards.front: Name the three mechanistic types of drug-resistant bacteria.
cards.back: Drug tolerant: the target changes so the drug binds poorly (for example altered RNA polymerase or penicillin-binding proteins). Drug destroying: an enzyme inactivates the drug (beta-lactamases, aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes). Drug impermeable: less drug gets in, through lost porins or active efflux pumps.

cards.front: What is the MBC, and what does a small versus large MBC-to-MIC gap indicate?
cards.back: MBC is the lowest concentration that kills 99.9% of the inoculum; it is judged by subculturing a clear tube into drug-free medium. If the MBC is close to the MIC, the drug is bactericidal. If it is far above the MIC, the drug is bacteriostatic. MBC is not used to choose drugs at the bedside.

cards.front: Which bactericidal antibiotics show concentration-dependent killing and which show time-dependent killing?
cards.back: Concentration-dependent: aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones. The rate and extent of killing rise with drug concentration, which (with their long postantibiotic effect) supports once-daily aminoglycoside dosing. Time-dependent: beta-lactams and vancomycin. Killing continues only while the serum level stays above the MBC, so the time above that level is what matters and divided doses are used.

cards.front: Classify: bacteriostatic versus bactericidal antimicrobials
cards.text: Primarily bactericidal: {{penicillins}}, {{cephalosporins}}, {{aminoglycosides}}, {{vancomycin}} and {{fluoroquinolones}}. Primarily bacteriostatic: {{sulfonamides}}, {{tetracyclines}}, {{chloramphenicol}}, {{erythromycin}} and {{clindamycin}}.

cards.front: Classify: antimicrobials by the organism they mainly act on
cards.text: Antifungal: {{griseofulvin}} and {{amphotericin B}}. Antiviral: {{acyclovir}}. Antiprotozoal: {{metronidazole}}. Anthelmintic: {{mebendazole}}. Antimycobacterial: {{ethambutol}}.

cards.front: Complete: superinfection organisms and treatment
cards.text: Candida albicans causes {{monilial diarrhoea and thrush}}, treated with {{nystatin}} or clotrimazole. {{Clostridium difficile}} causes pseudomembranous enterocolitis after clindamycin, tetracyclines, ampicillin and other drugs; KDT lists metronidazole or vancomycin, while GG14 now prefers oral {{vancomycin}} or {{fidaxomicin}}.

cards.front: Complete: specific prophylaxis indications
cards.text: Recurrence of rheumatic fever is prevented with {{benzathine penicillin}}. Tuberculosis contacts are protected with {{isoniazid}} for 6 months. Pneumocystis prophylaxis in AIDS or transplant patients uses {{cotrimoxazole}}. Dental extraction in valvular heart disease is covered with {{amoxicillin}} or clindamycin.

cards.front: How do sulfonamides stop bacterial growth, and why are human cells spared?
cards.back: Sulfonamides resemble PABA and competitively block dihydropteroate synthase, so the bacterium cannot make folate. Human cells take preformed folate from the diet and are unaffected. Excess PABA reverses the effect.

cards.front: Name three bacterial routes to sulfonamide resistance.
cards.back: Increased PABA production; a folate synthase with low affinity for sulfonamides; or an alternative pathway that uses preformed folate taken up from the medium. Resistance to one sulfonamide usually means resistance to all of them.

cards.front: What causes sulfonamide crystalluria, and how is it prevented?
cards.back: The acetylated metabolite is less soluble than the parent drug, especially in acidic urine, so it can precipitate. Prevent it with high fluid intake and alkalinised urine. It is now infrequent.

cards.front: Why are sulfonamides avoided in neonates, and which patients risk haemolysis?
cards.back: They displace bilirubin from albumin, and the neonatal blood brain barrier is more permeable, so kernicterus can follow. Haemolysis occurs with high doses in G6PD-deficient people.

cards.front: What is the logic of combining trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole?
cards.back: It is a sequential block of folate synthesis: sulfamethoxazole blocks an early step and trimethoprim blocks bacterial dihydrofolate reductase. Each alone is static, but together they are often cidal. Trimethoprim is far more potent against the bacterial enzyme than the human one.

cards.front: What are the main current uses of cotrimoxazole?
cards.back: Uncomplicated and recurrent urinary tract infection, including prostatitis because trimethoprim concentrates in prostatic fluid; respiratory tract infection; Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (treatment and prophylaxis); chancroid as a second-line option. Its use for typhoid has largely been dropped.

cards.front: Why is cotrimoxazole avoided in pregnancy, and what can happen if it is given near term?
cards.back: Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist with a theoretical teratogenic risk, so it is avoided in pregnancy. Given near term it can cause neonatal haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia.

cards.front: How do fluoroquinolones kill bacteria, and why do they spare the host?
cards.back: They inhibit DNA gyrase (the main target in gram-negative bacteria) and topoisomerase IV (main target in gram-positive bacteria), so the bacterium cannot relax and separate DNA and dies. Human cells rely on topoisomerase II, which binds these drugs poorly.

cards.front: Complete: sulfonamide structure and cotrimoxazole ratio
cards.text: All sulfonamides derive from {{sulfanilamide}} and need a free {{para amino}} group for activity. Trimethoprim inhibits bacterial {{dihydrofolate reductase}}. A dose ratio of {{5:1}} (sulfamethoxazole to trimethoprim) gives a plasma ratio of about {{20:1}}.

cards.front: Complete: non-antibacterial uses of sulfonamides
cards.text: Sulfadoxine with {{pyrimethamine}} treats {{chloroquine-resistant falciparum malaria}}, {{Pneumocystis}} pneumonia in AIDS, and {{toxoplasmosis}}. Topical {{silver sulfadiazine}} is used to prevent infection in burns.

cards.front: Classify: quinolone generations and prototypes
cards.text: {{Nalidixic acid}} is an early quinolone that inhibits DNA gyrase and is now used mainly for urinary infection. {{Ciprofloxacin}} is the prototype first-generation fluoroquinolone. {{Levofloxacin}} and {{moxifloxacin}} are second-generation agents with better gram-positive and atypical activity.

cards.front: Complete: fluoroquinolone safety and interactions
cards.text: Fluoroquinolones risk {{tendon rupture}}, especially over {{60}} years of age or with {{corticosteroids}}. They are {{contraindicated}} in pregnancy. Ciprofloxacin raises levels of {{theophylline}} and {{warfarin}}. {{Antacids}} and iron reduce their absorption.

cards.front: How do beta-lactams kill bacteria?
cards.back: They acylate the transpeptidases (penicillin-binding proteins) that cross-link peptidoglycan, so the cell wall cannot be properly built. Growing cells become wall-deficient, swell osmotically and lyse, helped by autolysins. Human cells make no peptidoglycan, which explains their low toxicity.

cards.front: What are the three main ways bacteria resist penicillins?
cards.back: Beta-lactamase (penicillinase) that opens the lactam ring; altered penicillin-binding proteins, as in MRSA (PBP2a) and resistant pneumococci; and reduced entry through porins in gram-negative bacteria.

cards.front: Why is penicillin G given parenterally, and what limits its duration?
cards.back: Gastric acid destroys it, so less than a third of an oral dose is absorbed. Renal tubular secretion clears it rapidly; the adult half-life is about 30 minutes. Probenecid blocks tubular secretion and prolongs levels.

cards.front: What are the serious toxic effects of high-dose penicillin G?
cards.back: It is among the least toxic antibiotics, but very large i.v. doses (above about 20 MU) can cause confusion, twitching, convulsions and coma, especially with renal failure. High doses also impair platelet function. Intrathecal use is not recommended. Accidental i.v. procaine penicillin causes CNS stimulation.

cards.front: Name three infections for which penicillin G is still the drug of choice, and its role in diphtheria.
cards.back: Syphilis (all stages; benzathine penicillin for early and latent disease), leptospirosis, and streptococcal infections such as pharyngitis (with benzathine penicillin to prevent rheumatic fever recurrence). In diphtheria, antitoxin is the primary treatment; penicillin is only an adjunct, with procaine penicillin 1 to 2 MU daily for 10 days used to prevent the carrier state. Erythromycin is an alternative for both the acute illness and carriers, and some prefer it.

cards.front: How do procaine and benzathine penicillin G differ?
cards.back: Both are insoluble depot salts given deep i.m., never i.v. Procaine penicillin gives lower plasma levels that are sustained for 12 to 24 hours, with procaine-related toxicity. Benzathine releases penicillin very slowly, giving low but prophylactically useful levels for up to about 4 weeks.

cards.front: How common is penicillin hypersensitivity, and how severe can it be?
cards.back: About 1 to 10% of patients react. Penicillin G is the most commonly implicated drug. Procaine penicillin causes the most reactions since procaine is itself allergenic. Rash, urticaria and fever are common; anaphylaxis is rare (about 1 to 4 per 10,000) but can be fatal.

cards.front: After an immediate-type penicillin reaction, what other drugs should be avoided?
cards.back: Other penicillins, because cross-sensitivity is partial. Cephalosporins are also generally avoided after an immediate reaction. If the earlier reaction was only a rash, a penicillin may be given cautiously. Hyposensitisation is used only when no alternative exists.

cards.front: Why is a negative penicillin skin test not reassuring, and which test is safer?
cards.back: A negative intradermal test does not exclude delayed hypersensitivity, and penicillin skin testing can itself trigger fatal anaphylaxis. Benzylpenicilloyl-polylysine is the safer test. Penicillin antibodies alone do not mean allergy, since almost everyone treated makes them.

cards.front: How does clavulanic acid work, and which enzymes does it block?
cards.back: It is a suicide inhibitor: it binds beta-lactamase and is destroyed in the process, so the enzyme is inactivated. It blocks class II to V enzymes but not class I cephalosporinase. It has little antibacterial activity of its own and is combined with amoxicillin as co-amoxiclav.

cards.front: Why does piperacillin with tazobactam fail against some Pseudomonas?
cards.back: Tazobactam does not inhibit the inducible chromosomal beta-lactamase of Pseudomonas and other Enterobacteriaceae, and it cannot reverse loss of drug permeability. Clavulanate and sulbactam share this limitation.

cards.front: What defines fourth-generation cephalosporins, and name two.
cards.back: They keep high potency against Enterobacteriaceae with a third-generation-like spectrum, but resist hydrolysis by inducible chromosomal beta-lactamases. Examples: cefepime and cefpirome.

cards.front: What distinguishes fifth-generation cephalosporins?
cards.back: They are active against MRSA and penicillin-resistant pneumococci because they bind altered penicillin-binding proteins (such as PBP2a). Examples: ceftaroline fosamil and ceftobiprole medocaril. They are still vulnerable to some extended-spectrum beta-lactamases.

cards.front: What is aztreonam, and why is it useful in penicillin allergy?
cards.back: A monobactam with a narrow spectrum: it covers gram-negative enteric bacilli, H. influenzae and Pseudomonas, but not gram-positive cocci or anaerobes. It lacks cross-allergy with penicillins and cephalosporins, except ceftazidime, which shares a side chain with it.

cards.front: Complete: penicillin G properties
cards.text: Penicillin G is {{acid labile}}, has an adult plasma half-life of about {{30 minutes}}, and its renal excretion is blocked by {{probenecid}}. Its main resistance mechanism is {{penicillinase}} production.

cards.front: Classify: penicillin types
cards.text: Acid-resistant oral penicillin: {{penicillin V}}. Penicillinase-resistant: {{cloxacillin}} and {{dicloxacillin}}. Aminopenicillins: {{ampicillin}} and {{amoxicillin}}. Carboxypenicillin: {{ticarcillin}}. Ureidopenicillin: {{piperacillin}}.

cards.front: Classify: cephalosporin generations with examples
cards.text: First generation: {{cefazolin}} (parenteral) and {{cephalexin}} (oral). Third generation with Pseudomonas activity: {{ceftazidime}}. Fourth generation, resistant to inducible beta-lactamases: {{cefepime}}. Fifth generation with MRSA activity: {{ceftaroline}}.

cards.front: Complete: carbapenem and monobactam facts
cards.text: Imipenem is given with {{cilastatin}} to block {{dehydropeptidase I}} in the renal tubule, and it causes {{seizures}} more often than meropenem. {{Aztreonam}}, a monobactam, is generally safe in penicillin allergy; the exception to cross-sensitivity is {{ceftazidime}}.
